stories.headline: Trump Targets Sen. Cassidy and Rep. Massie After Indiana Primary Victories
stories.summary:
President Trump and his allies are training their sights on two prominent Republican critics — Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana and Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky — following decisive primary victories this week in Indiana. Trump-backed challengers defeated five of eight incumbent Indiana state senators who had opposed the president's push for congressional redistricting, with Trump-allied groups spending over $10 million on the races. One incumbent survived, and one race remained too close to call.

The Indiana results mark the first major test of Trump's endorsement power in the 2026 primary cycle, and the outcome reinforced his grip on the Republican Party. Cassidy, who voted to convict Trump in his 2021 Senate impeachment trial, and Massie, a persistent intraparty critic, are now considered primary targets as the president seeks to consolidate control ahead of the midterms. The Club for Growth, one of the groups backing Trump's preferred candidates, declared the Indiana results 'a big win for Trump.'

Supporters of Trump's approach argue the results demonstrate that voters in Republican-leaning states want elected officials who align with the president's agenda, particularly on redistricting that could yield additional GOP House seats. Critics, including more traditional conservatives, frame the purge as a punitive effort to enforce loyalty rather than advance principled policy, warning it could push the party toward ideological conformity at the expense of independent judgment.

The Indiana primaries are seen as a bellwether for a series of upcoming Republican nomination battles this month. Political observers say the scale of Trump's investment — and the results — signal that incumbents who have crossed the president face serious electoral risk, reshaping the calculus for Republican officeholders nationwide heading into the midterm cycle.

stories.headline: Update: WHO Chief Travels to Tenerife as Hantavirus-Hit Cruise Ship Arrives
stories.summary:
WHO Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus traveled personally to Tenerife to oversee the arrival of the MV Hondius, a cruise ship carrying passengers affected by a hantavirus outbreak. The vessel, which docked in the early hours of Sunday at the port of Granadilla, had six confirmed cases among its passengers, including one of the three who died during the voyage from South America. Ghebreyesus issued a direct public message to Tenerife residents: 'This is not another Covid. The current public health risk from hantavirus remains low.'

Passengers aboard the MV Hondius are being held on the vessel and will only disembark onto smaller boats when repatriation flights are ready on the tarmac. Flights are arranged to return passengers to the UK, US, France, Germany, Belgium, and Ireland, with the EU sending additional aircraft for European citizens. A WHO expert and two Dutch physicians aboard the ship are conducting medical assessments and report no new symptomatic passengers.

The ship's arrival in the Canary Islands was contentious. The president of the Canary Islands region opposed it, questioning why the final response phase could not have taken place in Cape Verde, the ship's previous stop. The far-right party Vox launched political attacks against Spain's central government over the decision, while local protests were reported. Spanish Health Minister Mónica García defended the containment precautions in detail at a news conference.

Hantaviruses are typically carried by rodents, and the WHO believes passengers contracted the Andes strain — which allows limited human-to-human transmission — while in South America. Symptoms can include fever, extreme fatigue, muscle aches, and shortness of breath. The Tenerife arrival represents a significant logistical and public health operation, with international attention heightened by lingering public anxiety stemming from the COVID-19 pandemic.

stories.headline: Iran Sets Conditions for World Cup Participation Amid U.S.-Iran Tensions
stories.summary:
Iran's Football Federation has indicated the national team will compete at this summer's World Cup but has presented FIFA with at least 10 conditions for participation, including guaranteed visas for all players, coaches, and officials — including those who completed military service with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The IRGC is designated a terrorist organization in both the United States and Canada, and the federation's president was denied entry to Canada before last month's FIFA Congress, with his IRGC links cited as the reason.

Iran is also demanding respect for its flag and national anthem, enhanced security at airports, hotels, and stadiums, and restrictions on journalists asking questions beyond 'technical football matters.' The World Cup begins June 11 across the United States, Mexico, and Canada. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Iranian footballers would be welcome but warned individuals with IRGC links could still face entry restrictions, leaving FIFA in a delicate position between sporting inclusivity and national security policy.

The demands come against the backdrop of ongoing U.S.-Iran military hostilities, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. A fragile ceasefire has largely suspended the fighting, but diplomatic relations remain deeply strained. The situation is further complicated by an incident at the women's Asian Cup in March when several Iranian players attempted to claim asylum in Australia, triggering a diplomatic standoff.

FIFA faces a structural challenge: it can influence tournament logistics and official protocols, but visa decisions and border security remain under U.S. and Canadian jurisdiction. The federation's statement that Iran will compete 'without any retreat from our beliefs, culture and convictions' signals that political tensions are likely to shadow the team's participation throughout the tournament.

stories.headline: Baseball Hall of Famer Bobby Cox, Longtime Atlanta Braves Manager, Dies at 84
stories.summary:
Bobby Cox, the Hall of Fame manager who led the Atlanta Braves to 14 consecutive division titles and the franchise's only World Series championship in 1995, died Saturday at age 84. The Braves confirmed his death; details on the cause were not immediately available. Cox had suffered a stroke in 2019.

Cox took over a last-place Braves team in June 1990 and engineered a worst-to-first turnaround in 1991, launching an unprecedented run of divisional dominance that no professional sports franchise in any league has matched. He managed the team for 25 years, leading Atlanta to five National League pennants before retiring after the 2010 season. He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 2014.

'Bobby was the best manager to ever wear a Braves uniform,' the team said in a statement. 'His Braves managerial legacy will never be matched.' Cox was known for his calm dugout demeanor and loyalty to his players, as well as holding the all-time record for ejections in Major League Baseball history — a mark worn as a badge of honor by his supporters.

stories.headline: Update: Peter Magyar Sworn In as Hungary's Prime Minister, Ending Orbán's 16-Year Rule
stories.summary:
Péter Magyar was officially sworn in as Hungary's new prime minister on Saturday at the Parliament building in Budapest, formally ending Viktor Orbán's 16-year authoritarian tenure. Magyar's center-right Tisza party secured a historic parliamentary majority in last month's election, winning more votes and seats than any party in Hungary's post-Communist history.

Magyar, a former opposition leader and one-time Orbán ally who turned fierce critic, now faces the formidable task of overhauling what Orbán called an 'illiberal democracy' — including a judiciary, media landscape, and public institutions widely seen as reshaped in Fidesz's image over more than a decade. The swearing-in ceremony marks the concrete institutional transfer of power following the election result covered in previous days.

Hungary's political transformation carries significant implications for the European Union, which had long been in conflict with Orbán over rule-of-law standards and his government's alignment with Russia and China. Magyar has signaled a return to closer EU cooperation, though the scale of institutional reform needed means his early months in office will be closely watched by Brussels and NATO allies alike.

stories.headline: UK Deploys Warship to Middle East for Potential Hormuz Escort Mission
stories.summary:
The United Kingdom announced Saturday that it is moving a warship to the Middle East as part of contingency planning for a European-led mission to escort commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. The deployment is conditional on a stable ceasefire taking hold in the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict that has disrupted shipping in the region.

The move reflects growing European concern about freedom of navigation through one of the world's most critical maritime chokepoints, through which roughly 20 percent of global oil trade passes. A coalition of European nations has been discussing a joint escort operation modeled on earlier Gulf security arrangements, though the diplomatic and military parameters remain under negotiation.

The announcement comes as the U.S. and Iran have been edging toward a short-term deal to halt hostilities, and follows days of naval clashes in the strait involving U.S. destroyers. Britain's deployment signals that Western allies are preparing for a post-ceasefire security architecture even before a formal agreement is reached.

stories.headline: Jack Smith Accuses DOJ of Corruption in Fiery Private Remarks, Targeting of Trump Critics
stories.summary:
Former special counsel Jack Smith delivered an unusually sharp rebuke of the Justice Department at a private Washington dinner in April, remarks that have since become public. Smith accused the DOJ of being 'corrupted' and said it is 'targeting people for criminal prosecution simply because the president doesn't like them,' citing ongoing investigations into former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James.

Smith's remarks drew a swift response from a DOJ spokesperson, who told Fox News Digital that the department 'expected nothing less from Jack Smith whose sole mission was to politically prosecute a former president.' The spokesperson added that 'this DOJ has ended the weaponization perpetrated by the Biden Administration and will continue to ensure no one is above the law.'

The exchange underscores a deepening institutional conflict between Trump's Justice Department and critics who argue it is being used to settle political scores. Smith himself prosecuted Trump on charges related to the 2020 election and classified documents before both cases were dropped; Republicans have long accused Smith of the same 'weaponization' he now alleges against the current DOJ. The episode raises fresh questions about prosecutorial independence and the politicization of federal law enforcement from both ends of the political spectrum.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Fires on Iranian Oil Tankers as Ceasefire Strains, Awaits Tehran Response
stories.summary:
U.S. fighter jets struck two Iran-flagged oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, accusing them of attempting to violate the American naval blockade by docking at an Iranian port. The strikes came as the United States simultaneously awaited Iran's response to a draft deal to end the nearly 10-week-old war. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington expected to hear from Tehran imminently, while Iran's foreign minister accused the U.S. of breaching the month-old ceasefire and undermining diplomacy.

The Pentagon released footage of the strikes on the tankers. Vice President Vance met Friday in Rome with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman al-Thani, a key back-channel mediator, as formal negotiations between the U.S. and Iran continue through Pakistan. President Trump stated that the ceasefire remains technically in effect and that his proposal includes conditions that would prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

Iran charged that U.S. forces attack every time a diplomatic solution appears within reach. The clashes represent the most serious flare-up since the ceasefire was announced last month, raising doubts about its durability. Analysts say the U.S. blockade is squeezing Iranian oil exports so severely that the regime may be dumping crude into the Persian Gulf as storage capacity runs out.

The U.S. also imposed new sanctions on three Chinese firms for providing satellite imagery to Iran that enabled Iranian military strikes on American forces. Meanwhile, Rubio urged European allies in Rome to move beyond rhetoric and take concrete action against Iran, as the Trump administration seeks to build international pressure ahead of any potential deal.

stories.headline: Virginia Supreme Court Strikes Down Democratic Redistricting Plan, Reshaping Midterm Landscape
stories.summary:
The Virginia Supreme Court ruled 4-3 on Friday to invalidate a voter-approved Democratic congressional redistricting plan, delivering a major blow to the party's hopes of flipping the U.S. House in this fall's midterm elections. The majority held that the Democratic-led legislature violated procedural requirements when it placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot, rendering the April 21 referendum result null and void. Democrats had expected the redrawn maps to net as many as four additional U.S. House seats.

The ruling, combined with a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision that severely weakened the Voting Rights Act, has significantly expanded Republicans' congressional gerrymandering advantage heading into the midterms. President Trump celebrated the decision on social media, calling it a 'huge win for the Republican Party, and America.' NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson said Republicans are 'on offense' and will win the House majority.

Virginia Democrats quickly announced plans to file an emergency appeal with the U.S. Supreme Court. Democratic Speaker Don Scott and Senator Mark Warner condemned the ruling, with Warner saying 'justice was not served in Virginia' and that the decision overrode the will of voters. Democrats noted that the state spent $5.2 million on the referendum that has now been thrown out.

The decision is the latest in a string of redistricting setbacks for Democrats across multiple states. Republicans are pressing advantages in Alabama and elsewhere following recent court rulings, while Democrats acknowledge their path to recapturing the House has become significantly narrower. Political analysts say the midterm playing field is now tilted more heavily toward Republicans than it appeared even two weeks ago.

stories.headline: Trump Set to Fire FDA Commissioner Makary Amid Agency Turmoil
stories.summary:
Multiple news outlets reported Friday that President Trump is preparing to dismiss Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Marty Makary, a Make America Healthy Again advocate installed as FDA head last year. The Wall Street Journal, which broke the story, reported that Trump grew personally frustrated over what he viewed as Makary's slow pace in approving flavored vaping products, a top priority the president pledged to advance in his second term.

Makary has faced criticism from multiple directions throughout his tenure. Pharmaceutical industry groups have complained about dysfunction at the agency, while anti-abortion groups criticized him for declining to further restrict access to mifepristone, the medication used for medication abortions. Internally, Makary increasingly relied on a small inner circle of advisers, generating conflicts with the Department of Health and Human Services and the White House.

The reported firing has not been confirmed by the White House, and officials indicated Trump could still change his mind. The FDA oversees the approval of drugs, vaccines, and medical devices, making the leadership of the agency consequential for the pharmaceutical industry and public health policy alike. The agency approved blueberry- and mango-flavored vapes for the first time in years earlier this week, seen as a move to satisfy Trump's agenda.

Makary's potential dismissal would mark another significant leadership change at a major federal health agency under the Trump administration. The turmoil at the FDA has raised questions among health policy experts about the stability of drug approval processes and regulatory oversight during a period of significant policy change.

stories.headline: Australian By-Election Could Deliver One Nation Its First Federal Lower House Seat
stories.summary:
Votes were being counted Saturday in the Australian federal by-election for the seat of Farrer in New South Wales, with the contest viewed as a significant test of support for the right-wing populist One Nation party. One Nation has never won a seat in Australia's federal House of Representatives, but polling suggested a competitive three-way race among the Liberal Party candidate, independent Michelle Milthorpe, and One Nation's David Farley, a former CEO of Australia's largest beef producer.

The by-election was triggered by the resignation of Sussan Ley, who quit after being ousted as the Liberal Party leader following nine months in the role. The contest is the first federal electoral test for the new leaders of both the Liberal and National parties, which suffered their worst-ever combined defeat at last year's federal election and have struggled with infighting and poor polling since.

One Nation recorded the second-highest vote share of any party in the South Australian state election in March, its best-ever electoral result. A Farley victory in Farrer would mark a historic breakthrough for the party, which has operated primarily as a senate presence under longtime leader Pauline Hanson. The result would not affect the Labor government's parliamentary majority but could signal a shift in Australia's political landscape toward right-wing populism.

The by-election also carries symbolic significance as the first time neither Labor nor the Liberal-National Coalition may make the final two-candidate count in a federal contest. Farrer is a vast rural electorate covering 127,000 square kilometers in inland New South Wales, and has been held exclusively by the Liberal or National parties throughout its history.

stories.headline: Update: Starmer Refuses to Resign After Labour Suffers Historic Local Election Losses to Reform UK
stories.summary:
British Prime Minister Keir Starmer declared Friday he would not resign despite his Labour Party losing more than half the seats it was defending in English local and regional elections, calling the results "very tough" and saying he was "not going to walk away." Reform UK, led by Nigel Farage, swept hundreds of council seats across traditional Labour strongholds in England's north — including Sunderland — and made significant gains from Conservatives in areas such as Essex, marking the party's most consequential electoral performance to date.

The elections were widely interpreted as a referendum on Starmer's leadership less than two years after Labour won power by a landslide, ending 14 years of Conservative government. Voters signaled impatience over slow economic improvement and a perceived failure to deliver meaningful change. Welsh Labour leader Eluned Morgan resigned after her party suffered heavy losses in Wales, adding to the pressure on Starmer's national leadership.

Farage framed the results as a mandate against the political establishment, with Reform running on anti-immigration and anti-establishment themes. Conservatives, led by Kemi Badenoch, also claimed modest victories, including taking Westminster City Council from Labour. Starmer's supporters argue he inherited deep structural problems and that reforms take time; critics within Labour warn the party faces an existential threat from Reform on one flank and the Conservatives on another.

This is a new development on a previously covered story: results are now largely confirmed, Starmer has publicly responded, and Welsh Labour's leader has resigned — all material changes since earlier coverage of the vote count.

stories.headline: Update: Australian Women Formally Charged with Crimes Against Humanity After Return from Syria
stories.summary:
Two Australian women with alleged links to the Islamic State appeared in a Melbourne court Friday and were remanded in custody after being charged with crimes against humanity. Kawsar Ahmad, 53, faces four counts, with police alleging she travelled to Syria in 2014 and kept a female slave in her home purchased for $10,000; her daughter Zeinab Ahmad, 31, faces two similar charges carrying a maximum sentence of 25 years. A third woman, Janai Safar, 32, appeared separately in Sydney charged with entering a declared conflict zone and membership in a terrorist organization.

The three women were among a group of 34 Australian women and children who had been held at the al-Roj camp in northeastern Syria since 2019. The group departed the camp in February to return to Australia but was initially turned back before ultimately being permitted to fly home Thursday. The Australian Federal Police stated the investigation into all Australians who traveled to declared conflict zones remains active.

This is a material update on a previously covered story: the women have now appeared in court, formal charges have been filed, and remand decisions have been issued — concrete legal developments beyond the earlier reporting of their arrest.

stories.headline: Forecasters Warn Potentially Record-Breaking El Niño Could Bring Extreme Heat, Drought, and Floods
stories.summary:
Climate scientists and meteorologists warned Friday that a potentially historic El Niño event is expected to develop by mid-2026, with the World Meteorological Organization citing rapidly rising sea-surface temperatures and high confidence in its onset. Subsurface warm water anomalies in the equatorial Pacific are among the largest on record, raising the possibility of a so-called "super El Niño" — the most intense classification — though forecasters cautioned the outcome is not guaranteed and spring models carry greater uncertainty.

El Niño redistributes heat across the planet, typically triggering above-average temperatures, intensified heat waves, and worsening drought in some regions while increasing atmospheric moisture and the risk of severe flooding in others. Across the United States, forecasters expect a hotter-than-normal summer with significant heat waves and more frequent thunderstorms in the Southwest. In the Atlantic, El Niño tends to suppress hurricane activity by competing with heat that would otherwise fuel tropical storms.

The event, if it materializes at full strength, could affect hundreds of millions of people globally through altered agricultural conditions, water supply, and extreme weather frequency. Climate scientist Daniel Swain of the California Institute for Water Resources said Friday the physical preconditions are "about as large as we've seen in the historical record," adding that "the potential is there for something genuinely remarkable."

stories.headline: Frontier Airlines Jet Strikes Pedestrian on Denver Runway, Suffers Engine Fire
stories.summary:
A Frontier Airlines flight preparing to depart Denver International Airport for Los Angeles struck an individual on runway 17L late Friday night, the airport and airline confirmed. The aircraft sustained an engine fire following the incident but was safely evacuated. The identity and condition of the person struck were not immediately available.

The incident prompted an emergency response at Denver International Airport. Federal aviation authorities were expected to investigate how an individual came to be on an active runway during departure operations. Frontier Airlines had not issued a full public statement on the circumstances as of late Friday.

Runway incursions and pedestrian access to active airfields are among the most serious safety concerns in commercial aviation, and the incident is likely to draw scrutiny from the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration.
